user.text:
The city counts its ranked-choice contests from the cast vote records that the ballot scanners of every precinct export, in /app/data. Write a Python script at /app/bin/tally.py that tallies every contest of /app/data/election.json round by round by the rules in /app/docs (start with /app/docs/overview.md) and writes the tally file described in /app/docs/output.md. It is run as `python3 /app/bin/tally.py INPUT_DIR OUTPUT_FILE`. Run it on /app/data and save the result as /app/out/tally.json.

From /app, `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .` runs the script on a few small elections, and `python tools/check_tally.py` compares /app/out/tally.json with the certified results of the current election. The script will also be run on other elections, with other contests, batches and ballots, so it must follow the documented rules rather than what the current files happen to contain. Use only the Python standard library. Do not change anything under /app/data, /app/docs, /app/tests or /app/tools.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.

# Ranked-choice tally: overview

The city elects its mayor, council members, school board and district
commissions by ranked-choice voting: a voter ranks candidates in order of
preference, and the count runs in rounds, eliminating the last candidate of
each round, until one candidate holds a majority. The ballot scanners at the
polling places export cast vote records in batches. The tally program reads
the election definition and every batch, and writes the round-by-round
results of every contest. This note says what goes in, what comes out and in
which order the work is done. The rules for each step live in their own
notes:

| Note | Covers |
|---|---|
| `election.md` | the election definition: contests, candidates, write-ins, the lot |
| `records.md` | the cast vote record files, batches and revisions, how marks are written |
| `counting.md` | how a ballot is read, when it counts for whom, the rounds |
| `output.md` | the tally file |
| `changelog.md` | what changed between versions of these rules |

Where this note and a numbered rule in another note seem to disagree, the
numbered rule wins. The rules apply to every election the same way: nothing in
them depends on a particular contest, precinct, batch or candidate.

## 1. Inputs

1.1 An input directory holds `election.json` (`election.md`) and a directory
`cvr/` with the batch files of every scanner (`records.md`).

1.2 The input directory of a real election night holds batches that must not
be counted: rescans that a later revision replaced, a test deck run before the
polls opened, boxes that were scanned twice and voided. `records.md` 3 says
which batches count.

## 2. Steps

1. Read the election definition (`election.md`).
2. Read every batch file and keep the batches that count (`records.md` 3).
3. Read each record of those batches into the rankings of one ballot in one
   contest (`records.md` 4 and `counting.md` 1).
4. For each contest, run the rounds (`counting.md` 2 and 3) until the contest
   has a winner or no ballot is left to count.

Then write the results of every contest to one file (`output.md`).

## 3. Terms

- A **ballot** is one voter's paper. It can hold several contests; each
  contest of a ballot is one **record** in a bat

## 1. Contests

1.1 `contests` lists every contest of the election, in the order the results
are written (`output.md` 1.2). A contest is listed even when no ballot of it
was cast or counted.

1.2 `id` is the contest id that records name (`records.md` 4.1).

1.3 `max_ranks` is the number of ranking columns the ballot prints for the
contest. Rankings past `max_ranks` are not part of the ballot
(`counting.md` 1.1).

## 2. Candidates

2.1 `candidates` lists the candidates printed on the ballot. `id` is unique
within the election. Ids are compared without regard to case and to spaces
around them: ` ma03` and `MA03` name the same candidate.

2.2 `status` is `active` or `withdrawn`. A withdrawn candidate withdrew after
the ballots were printed: the name is on the paper and voters mark it, but the
candidate takes no part in the count (`counting.md` 1.2).

## 3. Write-ins

3.1 `write_ins` lists the qualified write-in candidates: people who filed to
be counted when a voter writes their name in. A qualified write-in takes part
in the count like a printed active candidate, under its `id`.

3.2 A write-in mark (`records.md` 4.4) is a mark for a qualified write-in
when its text, compared as in 3.3, equals the `name` or one of the `aliases`
of that write-in. Any other write-in, including one that writes the name of a
printed candidate, is an unqualified write-in and is not a mark for anyone.

3.3 Write-in text is compared after three changes to both sides: every letter
is turned to lower case (Unicode case folding), every character that is
neither a letter nor a digit is turned into a space, and runs of spaces are
turned into one space, with none at either end. Nothing else is changed: in
particular accents stay, so `Inês` and `Ines` are different texts. For
example `R.M.  delgado` and `R. M. Delgado` compare equal; `Delgado, Rosa` and
`Rosa Delgado` do not, unless both are listed.

## 4. The lot

4.1 `lot_order` lists every candidate and qualified write-in of the contest,
in an order drawn by lot before the election. It is used only to break the
last tie of `counting.md` 3.4.
# Cast vote records

## 1. Files

1.1 Every regular file in `cvr/` whose name ends in `.csv` or `.jsonl` is one
batch file. Other files (`manifest.txt` with the checksums of the export, for
example) are not batch files.

1.2 The name of a batch file is a label the scanner chose. It says nothing
about the batch, its revision or its precinct; those are written inside the
file.

1.3 Batch files are UTF-8 text with lines ending in a line feed. Blank lines
carry nothing.

I wrote `/app/bin/tally.py` and ran it on `/app/data`. The result is saved at `/app/out/tally.json`, and both checks pass.

- **Unit tests:** `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .` ran 4 tests and all passed.
- **Certified results:** `python tools/check_tally.py` reported every contest matching, 7 of 7 contests and 31 of 31 rounds.

The script follows the rules in `/app/docs` rather than anything specific to this election. It uses only the standard library and reads only the input directory. I left `/app/data`, `/app/docs`, `/app/tests` and `/app/tools` unchanged.

I wrote `/app/STATUS.json` with status `success`.

I only tested against the three kinds of input I had: the four small test fixtures, the current election, and the checker's copy of it. A few cases the docs leave open are my own reading:

- **Skipped rankings:** only two skipped rankings in a row end a ballot. A passed-over ranking between two skipped ones breaks the run.
- **`|` in write-in text:** it is treated as a mark separator in CSV cells, so write-in text containing `|` would be split.
- **Accents:** write-in comparison does no Unicode normalization. A decomposed accent (a letter plus a combining mark) would be read as a space.
